Hemchandra.description: A young prince and warrior, son of a deposed king of Magadha, determined to reclaim his father's kingdom from the Yavana invaders.

Madhavacharya.description: A revered Brahmin and spiritual teacher (Acharya), mentor to Hemchandra, who guides him in both religious and political matters.

Mrinalini.description: A woman deeply loved by Hemchandra, whose whereabouts are kept secret by Madhavacharya to prevent her from distracting Hemchandra from his duties.

Digvijay.description: Hemchandra's loyal companion and boatman, who assists him in his travels.

Bakhtiyar Khilji.description: A historical figure, the Yavana (Turkic Muslim) general who led the conquest of Bengal and Magadha in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

Mother.description: Hemchandra's mother, who urges him to fulfill his duty as a prince and reclaim his kingdom.

Prayaga.description: An ancient and sacred city in India, now known as Prayagraj (Allahabad), famous for the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna rivers.

Ganga.description: The Ganges River, one of the holiest rivers in Hinduism.

Yamuna.description: A major river in northern India, also considered sacred in Hindu tradition.

Delhi.description: A historic city in northern India, which was a political center during the time of the Yavana invasions.

Yavan.description: A term used in medieval India to refer to foreign invaders, particularly Muslims of Turkic or Persian origin.

Magadha.description: An ancient kingdom in eastern India, historically significant and the homeland of Hemchandra.

Mathura.description: A sacred city in northern India, associated with the Hindu god Krishna.

Gauda.description: A historical region and city in Bengal, which was a major political and cultural center.

Navadwip.description: A town in Bengal, known as a center of learning and religious activity.

Yama.description: The Hindu god of death, whose abode symbolizes the afterlife.

ghat.description: A series of steps leading down to a river, often used for bathing or religious rituals.

Acharya.description: A title for a learned teacher or spiritual preceptor, especially in Hindu tradition.

hermitage.description: A secluded dwelling where ascetics or holy persons live in contemplation.

Brahmin.description: A member of the priestly caste in Hindu society, traditionally responsible for religious rituals and teaching.

holy ash.description: Sacred ash (vibhuti) used in Hindu rituals, often applied to the forehead as a mark of devotion.

quiver.description: A container used to hold arrows.

guru.description: A spiritual teacher or guide in Indian tradition.

Hrishikesh.description: A Brahmin from Lakshmanavati, he is the head of the household where Mrinalini is staying.

Manimalini.description: A close friend and confidante of Mrinalini, she shares a sisterly bond with her.

Lakshmanavati.description: A historical city in Bengal, once a prominent capital during the medieval period.

Yavanas.description: A term historically used in India to refer to foreign invaders, often specifically Muslims or Greeks, but here likely refers to the Muslim forces under Bakhtiyar Khilji.

signet ring.description: A ring bearing an engraved seal, used historically to authenticate documents or as a mark of identity.

Girijaya.description: A sixteen-year-old beggar girl with a melodious voice who sings for alms and converses with Mrinalini.

Vrindavan.description: A town in Uttar Pradesh, India, closely associated with the legends of Krishna and the gopis (milkmaids).

Shyamsundar.description: An epithet of Lord Krishna, meaning 'the beautiful dark one.'

Teetala.description: A rhythmic cycle (tala) used in Indian classical music.

Jayjayanti.description: A raga (melodic framework) in Indian classical music.

gopis.description: Milkmaids of Vrindavan, celebrated in Hindu mythology for their devotion to Krishna.

shyam.description: A term meaning 'dark' or 'dusky,' often used as an affectionate descriptor for Krishna or for a person's complexion.

kunda.description: A type of white flower (Jasminum pubescens) often used in poetic descriptions for its purity and beauty.

sandalwood.description: A fragrant wood used in religious rituals and as a cosmetic mark on the forehead in Hindu tradition.

first watch.description: An ancient timekeeping term referring to the first segment of the night, typically just after sunset.

Sarvadhan.description: A merchant in Lakshmanavati who provides Hemchandra with lodging during his stay in the city.

Hrishikesh Sharma.description: A Brahmin whose house is mentioned as the place where Mrinalini is staying.

Janaki.description: A reference to Sita, also called Janaki, from the Ramayana, invoked in a song by Girijaya.

Raghubir.description: A reference to Lord Rama, called Raghubir, from the Ramayana, mentioned in Girijaya's song.

Ashoka.description: A flowering tree native to the Indian subcontinent, often associated with love and longing in Indian literature.

Hrishikesh Brahmin.description: Refers to Hrishikesh Sharma, a Brahmin, indicating his caste and social status.

first watch of the night.description: An old way of dividing the night into segments; the first watch refers to the early part of the night, typically from 6 pm to 9 pm.

Byomkesh.description: Hrishikesh's son, depicted as ignorant and depraved, who attempts to force himself on Mrinalini.

Radhika.description: Mentioned by Byomkesh as his beloved, possibly a relative or another woman in the household.

Draupadi.description: A principal female character from the Indian epic Mahabharata, known for her virtue and suffering.

Jayadratha.description: A character from the Mahabharata who abducted Draupadi and was later defeated by Arjuna.

Arjuna.description: A heroic prince and warrior from the Mahabharata, renowned for his valor and archery skills.

salvation.description: In Hindu context, refers to moksha or liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

Brahmani.description: The wife of a Brahmin, or sometimes used to refer to a woman of the Brahmin caste.

trysting.description: A secret meeting, especially between lovers.

Yama’s Abode.description: A reference to the realm of Yama, the Hindu god of death, symbolizing the afterlife or death.

Nabadwip.description: A historic town in Bengal, renowned as a center of learning and religious activity, especially in medieval times.

alms.description: Charitable gifts, usually food or money, given to the poor or beggars.

Lord of Gauda.description: The reigning king of Gauda (Bengal), an aged monarch presiding over the royal court, responsible for defending his kingdom against external threats.

Pashupati.description: The chief minister of religion and religious authority in the court, often engaged in discussions about state and spiritual matters.

Damodar.description: The chief scholar (presiding scholar) of the court, responsible for interpreting scriptures and leading scholarly debates.

Halayudh.description: A former occupant of a seat of honor in the assembly, possibly a respected scholar or courtier, now replaced by a less discerning sycophant.

Brahmins.description: A Hindu caste traditionally associated with priesthood, scholarship, and religious rituals.

Aryavarta.description: A term from ancient Indian texts referring to the land of the Aryans, broadly corresponding to northern India.

Turks.description: Refers to the Muslim invaders from Central Asia, particularly the forces of Bakhtiyar Khilji who invaded Bengal in the 13th century.

Yavana.description: A historical term used in India to refer to foreign invaders, especially Greeks and later Muslims such as the Turks.

Vishnu Purana.description: A major Hindu scripture, one of the eighteen Mahapuranas, containing cosmology, mythology, and legends.

Manu.description: Refers to the legendary progenitor of mankind in Hindu tradition and the attributed author of the Manusmriti.

Manusmriti.description: An ancient Hindu legal text, also known as the Laws of Manu, which outlines social and legal codes.

Saraswati.description: The Hindu goddess of knowledge, music, and the arts, often invoked as the patron of scholars.

Jagadishwara.description: A Sanskrit term meaning 'Lord of the Universe', often used as an epithet for God in Hinduism.

dais.description: A raised platform in a hall or large room, used for seats of honor or a throne.

kusa grass.description: A sacred grass in Hindu rituals, used for making seats or mats during religious ceremonies.

Maharaj.description: A respectful term for a king or great ruler in India.

Maharajadhiraj.description: A Sanskrit honorific meaning 'King of Kings', denoting a sovereign of high rank.

satraps.description: Provincial governors or local rulers, a term borrowed from ancient Persian administration but used in Indian historical contexts.

Samanta.description: A feudal lord or nobleman, often serving as a vassal to a king in medieval India.

Anushtubh.description: A common meter in Sanskrit poetry, consisting of four lines of eight syllables each.

infantry.description: Soldiers marching and fighting on foot; in this context, refers to the foot soldiers of the army.

brigands.description: Bandits or robbers, often used for groups engaged in plundering during times of war or unrest.

Janardana.description: An aged Brahmin living in Nabadwip, rendered nearly helpless by old age and deafness.

Digvijaya.description: A servant of Hemchandra, tasked with communicating Hemchandra's wishes to Janardana.

Manoroma.description: A young woman, described as beautiful and gentle, who is the granddaughter of Janardana and helps communicate with him.

Ganges.description: A sacred river in India, considered holy in Hinduism and significant in Bengali culture.

veena.description: A classical Indian stringed musical instrument, known for its melodious sound.

Nadiya.description: Another name for Nabadwip, often used interchangeably to refer to the region famous for its religious and cultural heritage.

Shyam.description: A poetic name for Lord Krishna, a major deity in Hinduism, often invoked in devotional songs and poetry.

maidservant.description: A female domestic worker or attendant, often serving in noble or wealthy households.

garland.description: A decorative wreath or string of flowers, often used in Indian culture for adornment or as offerings in religious ceremonies.

Bhagirathi.description: A major distributary of the Ganges River in Bengal, often referenced in Bengali literature.

Bengal.description: A historical region in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent, the primary setting of the novel.

kash-grass.description: A tall, white-flowered grass (Saccharum spontaneum) that blooms in Bengal during autumn, often associated with the season's beauty.

Manorama.description: A young woman who appears mysteriously by the tank at night; she is familiar with Hemchandra and displays both boldness and knowledge of the Turks.

Turk.description: Refers to the Turkish invaders, specifically the soldiers of Bakhtiyar Khilji who invaded Bengal in the early 13th century.

Turkish army.description: The invading military force of the Turks, representing the foreign threat to Bengal during this historical period.

banyan.description: A type of large fig tree (Ficus benghalensis) known for its aerial roots and cultural importance in India.

tank.description: A man-made pond or reservoir, often used for bathing, irrigation, or religious purposes in South Asia.

royal road.description: A main or principal road, often referring to a major highway used by royalty or armies.

garden house.description: A house situated within or near a garden, often used as a retreat or residence by nobility.

riverbank.description: The land alongside a river; in this context, it refers to the area beside the tank or water body.

stairway.description: A set of steps, often stone, leading down to the water's edge at a tank or river.

turbaned.description: Wearing a turban, a traditional head covering commonly worn by men in South Asia and the Middle East.

Keshav.description: A Bengali Brahmin who lived in Kashi and was the father of Haimavati; he mysteriously disappeared with his daughter after her marriage to Pashupati.

Haimavati.description: The eight-year-old daughter of Keshav who was married to Pashupati but vanished with her father on the wedding night.

Muhammad Ali.description: A Muslim envoy and confidant of the Turkic commander, Bakhtiyar Khilji, who negotiates with Pashupati regarding the fate of Gauda.

Gaur.description: Another name for Gauda, the capital city and kingdom in Bengal.

Sena dynasty.description: The ruling Hindu dynasty of Bengal during the late 12th and early 13th centuries, overthrown by Muslim invaders.

Kashi.description: The ancient city of Varanasi, a major center of Hindu learning and pilgrimage in northern India.

Bihar.description: A region and province in eastern India, neighboring Bengal, known for its historical significance.

Khilji.description: Refers to Bakhtiyar Khilji, the Turkic Muslim commander who invaded Bengal and conquered Gauda.

Qutb-ud-din.description: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, the first Sultan of Delhi and a prominent figure in the establishment of Muslim rule in India.

Muhammad Ghori.description: A prominent Muslim ruler and conqueror whose campaigns led to the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate.

tributary.description: A subordinate ruler or state that pays tribute to a more powerful sovereign or empire.

Mohammad Ali.description: A character associated with the Yavana (Muslim) forces, whose movements are being watched by Pashupati and his allies.

Shantashil.description: A loyal spy and agent of Pashupati, skilled in disguise and espionage, who brings intelligence about the Yavana camp.

vina.description: A traditional South Asian stringed musical instrument, known for its melodious sound.

obeisance.description: A gesture of deep respect or submission, such as bowing or prostrating oneself.

champa.description: A reference to the champa (or champak) flower, known for its golden color and fragrance, often used in poetic descriptions of beauty.

tresses.description: Long locks or strands of hair, often used in poetic descriptions.

braid.description: A hairstyle formed by interweaving three or more strands of hair.

creeper.description: A type of climbing plant, often used metaphorically in Indian literature to describe graceful movement.

jackal.description: A wild animal native to South Asia, often appearing in Indian folklore and metaphors.

abode.description: A dwelling place or home, here referring to the temple or residence of the goddess.

Ballal Sen.description: Referenced as a historical figure, Ballal Sen was a king of Bengal known for instituting the system of Kulinism.

Kulinism.description: A social system established by Ballal Sen in Bengal, which classified Brahmins and Kayasthas into hierarchical ranks, affecting marriage and social status.

widow remarriage.description: The practice of a widow marrying again, which was socially taboo in traditional Hindu society of the time.

caste.description: A hereditary social class in Hindu society, dictating social status and occupation.

benefactor.description: A person who provides help or support, especially in a position of authority or patronage.

Bapiti.description: A place name mentioned as the location from which Hemchandra is coming.

mansion.description: A large and impressive house, often used in Indian literature to refer to the residence of a wealthy or noble person.

chamber.description: A private room, often used in historical or aristocratic contexts to refer to a room within a large house or palace.

great forest.description: A significant location north of the city where the Yavana army has set up camp; likely a large, dense forest near the main setting.

camp.description: Refers to the military encampment of the Yavana forces near the city.

thief-catcher.description: A term for someone who apprehends thieves; similar to a constable or detective in historical Indian society.

Hemachandra.description: A skilled warrior and one of the main protagonists, Hemachandra is depicted here defending himself against attackers and struggling with his wounds.

Mrinal.description: Referenced in the song at the end, Mrinal is a central character in the novel, often associated with themes of fate and suffering.

Ratnamoyee.description: The young daughter of the boatman’s wife, Ratnamoyee shares a room with Mrinalini and Girijaya and is friendly and playful with them.

Patni.description: Refers to the boatman’s wife, whose house provides shelter to Mrinalini and her friends; 'Patni' is a Bengali term for a boatman's wife.

banyan tree.description: A large, sacred fig tree native to India, often associated with shelter and gathering places in Indian culture.

spear.description: A traditional pole weapon used in warfare, commonly carried by warriors in medieval India.

durva.description: A type of sacred grass (Cynodon dactylon) used in Hindu rituals and believed to have healing properties.

sacred thread.description: A reference to the 'yajnopavita', a ceremonial thread worn by upper-caste Hindus, here used metaphorically for a bandage.

ghee.description: Clarified butter commonly used in Indian cooking and rituals.

Braja.description: A sacred region in northern India associated with the childhood of Krishna, often referenced in devotional poetry.

Madhava.description: A name for the Hindu god Krishna, frequently invoked in songs and poetry.

tamala.description: A type of tree (Diospyros tomentosa) with dark leaves, often mentioned in Indian poetry for its beauty.

bandages.description: Strips of cloth used to bind wounds; here, referring to Hemchandra's injury.

King Sena.description: Refers to the reigning monarch of the Sena dynasty, the ruling Hindu dynasty of Bengal during the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

Bhadra.description: A month in the Bengali calendar, typically corresponding to August-September, associated with the monsoon season.

Krishna.description: A major deity in Hinduism, often invoked as a symbol of love and divine play.

Puranas.description: Ancient Hindu texts containing mythological stories, religious teachings, and cultural lore.

Bhagiratha.description: A legendary king in Hindu mythology who is credited with bringing the river Ganges down to earth through his penance.

usurper of religion.description: A phrase referring to someone who illegitimately claims religious authority or manipulates religion for personal gain.

champak.description: A fragrant flowering tree (Michelia champaca) native to South Asia, whose blossoms are often used as a metaphor for beauty.

lotus feet.description: A devotional term in Hinduism referring to the feet of a deity, symbolizing purity and divinity.

conqueror of death.description: An epithet for the Hindu god Shiva, who is believed to have mastery over death.

widow.description: A woman whose husband has died; in traditional Hindu society, widows were subject to strict codes of conduct regarding chastity and remarriage.

Patani.description: Refers to a woman of Pathan (Afghan Muslim) descent or household, indicating the presence of diverse communities in the setting.

Radhe.description: A devotional exclamation referring to Radha, the beloved of Krishna, often repeated in songs and prayers.

Vyomkesh.description: A character described as the disgrace of the Brahmin line, suspected by Hemchandra of being involved with Mrinalini.

prahar.description: An ancient Indian unit of time, roughly equivalent to three hours.

yojana.description: An ancient Indian unit of distance, approximately 8-9 miles (13-15 kilometers).

Dronacharya.description: A legendary teacher and warrior from the Indian epic Mahabharata, known for his martial prowess and tragic downfall.

Ashwatthama.description: The son of Dronacharya in the Mahabharata, whose supposed death led to Dronacharya's defeat.

bakul.description: A type of fragrant flowering tree (Mimusops elengi) commonly found in South Asia.

Urnanabha.description: A rare and reclusive figure, likened to a savior who could have rescued Gauda; the name is used metaphorically here.

Shantashila.description: Pashupati's right-hand man, responsible for carrying out secretive tasks and relaying information.

Damodar Sharma.description: A cunning agent involved in manipulating court affairs, particularly by altering manuscripts and advising the king.

Madansen.description: A courtier or informant who returns from Kashi and provides the king with information about the Yavana king's representative.

envoys.description: Messengers or representatives sent on a diplomatic mission.

tribute.description: A payment or gift made by one ruler or state to another, often as a sign of dependence or submission.

manuscript.description: A handwritten document, often of literary or historical significance.

scriptures.description: Sacred religious texts, especially those of Hinduism in this context.

pilgrimage.description: A religious journey to a sacred place, undertaken for spiritual reasons.

Janardana Sharma.description: Described as the foremost of the Kulinas, he is Manoroma's grandfather and a figure of authority in her family.

Jagadamba.description: A name for the Divine Mother or Goddess, often used in Hinduism to refer to the supreme goddess.

Eight-Armed One.description: A reference to a form of the Hindu goddess, likely Durga, who is depicted with eight arms.

Jagadishwari.description: Another epithet for the Goddess, meaning 'Mistress of the Universe' in Sanskrit.

Kulina.description: A high-status subgroup within the Brahmin caste, known for strict adherence to lineage and purity.

Shrotriya.description: A Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and qualified to perform religious rituals.

salutations.description: Formal acts of respect or worship, often involving gestures or prayers.

lineage.description: A line of descent or ancestry, particularly important in caste and family status.

scriptural.description: Relating to religious scriptures or authoritative sacred texts.

Keshab.description: Manorama's father, who, fearing an ill omen predicted by astrologers, takes steps to protect his daughter after her marriage.

Janardhan.description: Referred to as the Acharya, Janardhan is the spiritual teacher entrusted with Manorama's care after her father's death.

Prayag.description: An ancient and sacred city in India, now known as Allahabad, famous for its religious significance and confluence of rivers.

deity.description: A god or goddess; a divine being worshipped in the temple.

Minhaj-ud-din.description: A historian of the Yavanas who, six years after the events, records the history of the conquest.

King of Gauda.description: The reigning monarch of the kingdom of Gauda, depicted here as elderly and powerless during the invasion.

Vanga.description: An ancient region of Bengal, often paired with Gauda to refer to the broader area of Bengal.

Sonargaon.description: A historic city in Bengal, often serving as a refuge or secondary capital during times of crisis.

Suvarnagram.description: A place referenced as a destination for the fleeing royal family, possibly another name for a city or region in Bengal.

Morkataka.description: The place associated with Bakhtiyar Khilji, possibly his place of origin or base.

scimitar.description: A curved, single-edged sword of Middle Eastern or Central Asian origin, commonly used by warriors such as the Yavanas.

postern gate.description: A small, secondary gate in a fortification or palace, often used for secret or emergency exits.

Dharmadhikari.description: A high-ranking Hindu religious and administrative leader in Bengal, central to the story's conflict with Bakhtiyar Khilji.

Islam.description: The monotheistic religion founded by the Prophet Muhammad, followed by Bakhtiyar Khilji and his forces.

Sanatan Dharma.description: A term for the eternal, traditional Hindu faith, contrasted here with Islam.

Quran.description: The holy scripture of Islam, referenced by Bakhtiyar Khilji as the source of true faith.

Muhammad.description: The Prophet of Islam, mentioned as the figure to be worshipped according to Bakhtiyar Khilji.

Clive Sahib.description: Refers to Robert Clive, a British colonial officer known for his role in the conquest of Bengal in the 18th century.

envoy.description: A diplomatic representative sent to negotiate or communicate between parties.

treaty.description: A formal agreement between two or more parties, especially between states or rulers.

initiated.description: Formally admitted or introduced into a group or religion, often through a ritual.

Sultan.description: A Muslim sovereign or ruler, especially in the context of medieval India.

priest.description: A religious leader authorized to perform sacred rituals, here referring to an Islamic cleric.

guard.description: A person assigned to protect or detain someone, often as a soldier or watchman.

Banga Tiarak.description: A figure mentioned as having usurped the royal palace, contributing to the king's flight and the city's chaos.

Gauriya.description: Refers to things or people of Gaud (Gaur), an ancient region and kingdom in Bengal; here, it means the local soldiers.

Gaud.description: An ancient kingdom and region in Bengal, referenced as Vyomkesh's home and Mrinalini's former residence.

Shalagrama.description: Sacred stones, typically fossilized ammonite, worshipped by Hindus and associated with Vishnu; here, they are described as being desecrated during the invasion.

cavalrymen.description: Soldiers who fight mounted on horseback.

sacred threads.description: The 'yajnopavita', a sacred cord worn by Brahmin males as a symbol of their caste and religious duties.

leaf-cup.description: A small cup made from leaves, traditionally used in India for serving water or offerings.

Garjaya.description: A secondary character who appears to be present with Mrinalini and Girijaya, possibly another attendant or companion.

Kartik.description: A month in the Bengali (and Hindu) lunar calendar, typically falling in October-November, known for its cool weather and religious observances.

heretic.description: In this context, a term used to describe someone who is considered to have deviated from orthodox religious beliefs, often used pejoratively.

beggar woman.description: A term referring to a woman who is destitute and relies on alms for survival, often used to express humility or low status.

Sindhu.description: Refers to a breed of horse from the Sindh region, known for its strength and speed.

Hrishikesha.description: A character whose house Mrinalini left before coming to Navadwip; he is a figure from her past, possibly a guardian or protector.

Piyari.description: Mentioned as someone Digvijay hopes will come looking for him; possibly a nickname or alternate name for Girijaya.

bower.description: A pleasant, shaded retreat or shelter in a garden, often made with trees or climbing plants.

moustache.description: Facial hair grown on the upper lip; in this context, twisting the moustache is a gesture of pride or contemplation.

retreat in battle.description: A phrase meaning to withdraw or flee from a situation, often used metaphorically for escaping trouble.

Arundhati.description: Mrinalini’s elderly kinswoman and caretaker, who gives her away in marriage during the secret wedding.

Buddhist.description: A follower of Buddhism, a religious tradition originating in India; here, it denotes Mrinalini’s faith and social identity.

family priest.description: A religious officiant belonging to a family, responsible for conducting rituals such as marriage ceremonies.

maiden.description: An unmarried young woman, often used in historical or traditional contexts.

anoint you with turmeric.description: A reference to a traditional Indian pre-wedding ritual where turmeric paste is applied to the bride for auspiciousness and purification.

Bharat.description: The traditional Sanskrit name for India.

Kamarupa.description: An ancient kingdom located in present-day Assam and northeastern India, often depicted as a stronghold resisting invaders.

Aryan.description: Refers to the noble or warrior classes in ancient and medieval India, often used to denote the indigenous Hindu rulers.

India.description: The country in South Asia, here referenced in its historical context.

Kalika.description: A reference to the Hindu goddess Kali, or possibly a person named after her, whose word influenced Hemchandra's actions.

servitude.description: The state of being subject to domination or forced labor, here referring to subjugation under foreign rule.

vassal kings.description: Subordinate rulers who owe allegiance to a higher sovereign or king.

scripture.description: Sacred religious texts regarded as authoritative in Hindu tradition.

Gurudev.description: A respectful term meaning 'revered teacher' or 'spiritual master.'

Lion Gate.description: A specific gate of the city, likely a main entrance or exit, significant for its role in security and movement.

mlechchha.description: A Sanskrit term used to denote foreigners or those considered outside the traditional Hindu social order, often with a derogatory connotation.

Dharma Adhikari.description: A title meaning 'upholder of dharma (righteousness or religious law),' typically referring to a religious or judicial authority.

pyre.description: A pile of combustible material, often used for burning a corpse as part of funeral rites in South Asian traditions.

Durgadas.description: A Brahmin appointed to perform daily rituals for the eight-armed goddess; he leads the effort to recover the idol and perform Pashupati's funeral rites.

Ratnamayi.description: A friend of Girijaya who marries a merchant and resides in the new kingdom.

Ashtabhuja.description: A form of the goddess Durga depicted with eight arms, worshipped in Bengal.

widow-burning.description: Also known as 'sati,' the now-outlawed Hindu practice where a widow immolated herself on her husband's funeral pyre.

circumambulated.description: Walked around something (often a sacred object or fire) as a ritual act of respect or devotion.
